segments.text: <curious>Let's begin with the single biggest idea in this whole chapter.</curious> On the coordinate plane, geometry quietly turns into arithmetic.
Every question about shapes becomes a question about numbers — that is the whole power of Descartes' idea.
Ask how far one town sits from another, and the answer is just a subtraction followed by a square root, nothing more mysterious than that.
Picture the two towns as points. The horizontal gap and the vertical gap form a right triangle, and the straight-line distance is simply its hypotenuse.
Here is a lovely twist: if three points sit on one straight line, the triangle they form has zero area, and that zero is exactly the collinearity test we will lean on later.
Ask for the point one-third of the way along a highway, and that is the section formula doing its job.
So keep three tools close at hand: the distance between points, the point that divides a segment, and the area of a triangle.
Get fluent with these and everything later in Straight Lines is just careful bookkeeping.
Now the second big idea of this subtopic — the locus, which is simply the path traced by a moving point.
A locus is the set of every point that obeys one geometric rule, and nothing else.
Think of a goat tied to a peg by a rope. Its rule is 'stay five metres from the peg', so the path it can walk is a perfect circle.
Now take two villages and ask for the points that are equally far from both. Watch what that path turns out to be.
It is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them — a straight line, born purely from an equal-distance rule.
One caution from the edge cases: the external section formula divides by m minus n, so when m equals n it blows up, because that dividing point has run off to infinity.
And remember, translation of axes only slides the origin, it never rotates it, so slopes and distances stay exactly the same, only the coordinate labels change.
Almost every problem that says 'find the path of a point such that' is really a locus problem — turn the words into an equation and you are done.
Next, the area of a triangle from its three vertices — and the trick is trapezia.
Drop a perpendicular from each vertex down to the x-axis. Between the sides and the axis you get three trapezia.
The triangle's area is just the algebraic sum of these three trapezium areas — some added, some subtracted, depending on direction.
Writing each trapezium as half the sum of parallel sides times the width gives this three-term sum.
It looks messy, but expand every bracket and watch the clutter cancel.
What survives is one half the modulus of x one times y two minus y three, plus x two times y three minus y one, plus x three times y one minus y two — the formula you will use every time.
The modulus is doing real work here: it strips off the orientation sign so that area comes out non-negative, always.
And here is the payoff: if this area comes out as exactly zero, the three points cannot enclose anything — they lie on one straight line.
Let's put the toolkit to work with two quick classics.
First, find the centroid of the triangle with vertices A at two, minus three; B at minus four, five; and C at eight, one.
Just average coordinate by coordinate. The x-values two, minus four, eight sum to six; the y-values minus three, five, one sum to three; each divided by three.
That gives the centroid at two comma one. Done in a single step.
Second, are the points one comma four, three comma minus two, and minus three comma sixteen collinear? Do not chase three slopes — set the area to zero instead.
Plug into the area determinant: one times minus two minus sixteen, plus three times sixteen minus four, plus minus three times four minus minus two.
That is minus eighteen plus thirty six minus eighteen, and the modulus of that is zero.
Zero area means the three points lie in a row. Notice how the determinant did in one line what three slope checks would have done with three chances to slip a sign.
Now a two-step problem that chains our tools together.
The point P divides the segment from A at minus one, three to B at five, minus nine, with A P to P B equal to two to one. Find P, then its distance from the origin.
Since the division is internal, reach for the section formula with m to n equal to two to one.
The x-coordinate is two times five plus one times minus one, all over three; the y-coordinate is two times minus nine plus one times three, all over three.
That simplifies to nine over three and minus fifteen over three, giving P at three comma minus five.
With P known, the second half is just distance from the origin at zero, zero.
O P is the square root of three squared plus minus five squared, which is the square root of nine plus twenty five, that is root thirty four.
The lesson is the chaining: find the point with one tool, then measure with the next. Most multi-concept questions are exactly this.
<curious>Now a real locus problem — let's turn a sentence into a curve.</curious>
A point moves so that its distance from four comma zero is always twice its distance from one comma zero. Call the moving point P at h comma k.
Write the condition and square both sides to kill the roots: h minus four squared plus k squared equals four times the quantity h minus one squared plus k squared.
Now expand every bracket carefully and line the terms up.
The left side is h squared minus eight h plus sixteen plus k squared; the right side is four h squared minus eight h plus four plus four k squared.
Bring everything to one side. The minus eight h terms cancel, and what remains is three h squared plus three k squared minus twelve equals zero, so h squared plus k squared equals four.
Replace h comma k with x comma y and the locus is x squared plus y squared equals four — a circle of radius two centred at the origin.
Watch the tell: those linear minus eight h terms cancelling is the fingerprint of an Apollonius locus. Spot it early and you save yourself a page of algebra.

Scale the centroid: $x_1+x_2+x_3 = 3\bar{x}$ before solving for a missing vertex.

Pro-tip: for collinearity, the area determinant beats comparing slopes every time.
It never divides by zero and the modulus guards against orientation errors.
Get these cold and Straight Lines turns into bookkeeping.

Slope captures how steeply a line tilts — like a railway track climbing a valley.
Inclination $\theta$ is the anticlockwise angle from the $+x$-axis, with $0^\circ \le \theta < 180^\circ$.

segments.text: Before we leave foundations, let's lock in the mistakes examiners bank on.
Number one: internal versus external section. Internal uses m plus n in the denominator, external uses m minus n. Pick the wrong one and your point jumps to the wrong side.
Number two: never drop the modulus in the area formula. Without those bars you can report a negative area, and a negative area does not exist.
Number three: when a vertex is missing and you know the centroid, remember the sum of the three coordinates equals three times the centroid coordinate. Scale up by three first, then solve.
Number four: the shift of origin is new equals old minus shift, so capital X is x minus h and capital Y is y minus k. Adding instead of subtracting is the classic slip.
<whisper>And here is the pro-tip worth memorising: for any collinearity question, the area determinant beats comparing slopes, every single time.</whisper>
It never divides by zero, so no vertical-line worry, and the modulus quietly protects you from orientation sign errors.
Get all of this cold and, as promised, the rest of Straight Lines becomes pure bookkeeping.
Slope is the most-used idea in all of coordinate geometry, and wonderfully, one number does the whole job.
Picture walking a railway track climbing out of a valley: some stretches barely rise, others are steep. Slope is exactly that steepness, turned into a number.

Start from the positive x-axis and rotate anticlockwise until you point along the line. That rotation is the inclination theta, and by convention it lives from zero up to, but not including, one hundred eighty degrees.
Look at the three lines: a gentle one at thirty degrees, one falling to the right at one hundred thirty five degrees, and the dashed upright one at ninety degrees.
We convert that angle into a pure number with the tangent: slope m equals tan theta.

Why tangent? Because slope is rise over run, and that is exactly the tangent of the inclination. A forty five degree line has slope precisely one; a line heading downhill to the right has a negative slope.

There is exactly one place this breaks, and setters love it: the vertical line. Its inclination is ninety degrees, tan ninety does not exist, so its slope is undefined — never call it infinite, never call it zero.
Two quick reads: lines with equal slope point the same way and are parallel; lines whose slopes multiply to minus one meet at a right angle and are perpendicular.
Let's prove why slope equals rise over run — the whole formula sits inside one right triangle.
Take a rising line through P and Q. Drop a horizontal segment P N from P, and a vertical segment down from Q to meet it at N. That builds a right triangle, right-angled at N.
Because P N is parallel to the x-axis, the angle the line makes at P equals the inclination theta. The horizontal side P N is the run, and the vertical side Q N is the rise.
In that right triangle, tan theta is opposite over adjacent, which is Q N over P N, and that is y two minus y one over x two minus x one — rise over run.
If x one equals x two, the run collapses to zero, the triangle degenerates, theta becomes ninety degrees, and the slope is undefined. That is the vertical line showing up in the algebra.
Now perpendicularity. If two lines meet at a right angle, their inclinations differ by exactly ninety degrees, so take theta two as theta one plus ninety.
Then m two is tan of theta one plus ninety, and the identity turns that into minus cot theta one, which is minus one over m one.
Cross-multiply and you land on the clean condition: m one times m two equals minus one. That single line powers every perpendicular problem you will meet.
When two lines cross, how do we measure the angle between them from their slopes alone? Here is the tool.
A crossing actually makes two angles that add to one hundred eighty degrees — an acute one and its obtuse partner. The modulus in the formula is what selects the acute angle for us.
The formula: tan theta equals the modulus of m two minus m one over one plus m one m two.
Before you plug in, step one: glance for a vertical line. If one slope is undefined, this formula does not apply — handle it from inclinations directly.
Step two: compute one plus m one m two. If that comes out zero, the lines are perpendicular, the answer is ninety degrees, and you stop right there.
That is worth writing down: a zero denominator is not an error, it is precisely the perpendicular case, where tan theta blows up because theta is ninety degrees.
Step three, evaluate the ratio; step four, take the inverse tangent of that value to get the acute angle theta.
And if the question wants the obtuse angle instead, it is simply one hundred eighty degrees minus theta. One formula, both angles.
Two worked examples now — first a plain slope, then a perpendicular condition with a speed trap.
Example one: find the slope of the line through A at minus three, two and B at five, minus four, and say whether its inclination is acute or obtuse.
Two-point slope: minus four minus two over five minus minus three, which is minus six over eight, or minus three over four.
Since the slope is negative, the line falls to the right, so its inclination is obtuse — between ninety and one hundred eighty degrees.
Example two: the line through two, seven and k, one is perpendicular to the line through zero, minus three and four, five. Find k.
First the known line's slope: five minus minus three over four minus zero equals two. Perpendicular means flip and negate, so our line's slope is minus one half.

Set the first line's slope equal to that: one minus seven over k minus two equals minus one half. That gives minus six over k minus two equals minus one half, so k minus two is twelve, and k is fourteen.
The trap is forgetting the minus and writing plus one half, which lands on the planted answer minus ten. Flip and negate — perpendicular slopes always carry opposite signs.
Here is a two-part example that chains collinearity into the angle formula.
The points are P at one, one; Q at four, seven; and R at a comma a plus five. Part one: find a so that all three are collinear.
First anchor the slope of P Q: seven minus one over four minus one equals two.
For collinearity, the slope of P R must also be two. So a plus five minus one over a minus one equals two, giving a plus four equals two a minus two, which solves to a equals six.
So R is six comma eleven, and the whole line has slope two. Part two: what acute angle does it make with the line y equals x, whose slope is one?
Use the angle formula: tan theta is the modulus of one minus two over one plus two times one, which is the modulus of minus one third, that is one third.
So theta is the inverse tangent of one third, about eighteen point four three degrees.
Notice the structure: collinearity pinned down a, and only then did the angle formula finish the job. Chaining tools like this is the heart of the multi-concept questions.

board_events.text: Worked: A Line at 45° (Advanced)
Line $\ell$ makes $45^\circ$ with $3x - y + 5 = 0$, whose slope is $m_2 = 3$.
'$45^\circ$ with a line' works on either side — set the signed tangent to $\pm 1$.
Vertical check: $90^\circ$ vs $71.57^\circ$ gives $18.43^\circ \ne 45^\circ$ — no vertical solution.
Pitfalls: Slope & Angles
A vertical line's slope is UNDEFINED — not infinity, not zero.
Perpendicular means $m_1 m_2 = -1$, not $+1$ — keep the minus sign.
For 'a line making angle $\alpha$', use $\pm\tan\alpha$, not the modulus — two lines exist.
In Advanced problems, always check the vertical-line case separately.
Pro-tip: glance at geometry first — rising $\Rightarrow +$, falling $\Rightarrow -$, flat $\Rightarrow 0$, upright $\Rightarrow$ undefined.
That two-second sign check catches most arithmetic slips before they cost marks.
Slope is the workhorse of the whole chapter — keep these poles straight.
Six Costumes for One Line
A line is the simplest curve, yet it can wear six different forms.
Each form answers a different clue: a point and a direction, two points, the intercepts, or the distance from the origin.

Slope-intercept and point-slope cannot describe a vertical line — slope is undefined there.
Intercept form breaks for a line through the origin or parallel to an axis.
The real exam skill is translating fluently between forms, not memorising six.
Proof: Point-Slope Form
Take any point $(x,y)$ on a line of slope $m$ through the fixed point $(x_1,y_1)$.
The slope computed from those two points must equal $m$.
Put a second point $(x_2,y_2)$ in place of $m$ to get the two-point form.
Set $(x_1,y_1) = (0,c)$ and it collapses to $y = mx + c$.
Proof: Intercept & Normal Forms
Apply the two-point form to the intercepts $(a,0)$ and $(0,b)$.

Reducing $Ax+By+C=0$ to Normal Form
Move the constant across: $Ax + By = -C$.
Divide by $\pm\sqrt{A^2+B^2}$, choosing the sign so the right side is positive.
Pick the sign opposite to that of $C$ — a distance $p$ cannot be negative.
Fix $\omega$ from the signs of $\cos\omega$ and $\sin\omega$ together — never from one alone.
General form is the only form that never fails — your universal fallback.

segments.text: Now an Advanced-flavoured example where two things bite: the plus-or-minus, and the vertical line.
A line ell makes a forty five degree angle with the line three x minus y plus five equals zero. Rearranged, that line is y equals three x plus five, so its slope m two is three.
Here is the subtlety: making forty five degrees with a line can happen on either side of it, so we must not take the modulus blindly. Set the signed tangent equal to plus or minus one.
So m minus three over one plus three m equals plus or minus one — two equations, not one.
Take the plus one case: m minus three equals one plus three m, which gives minus two m equals four, so m is minus two.
Take the minus one case: m minus three equals minus one minus three m, which gives four m equals two, so m is one half.

Now the Advanced check most students skip: could a vertical line also work? A vertical line has inclination ninety degrees; the given line sits at about seventy one point five seven degrees, so the gap is about eighteen point four degrees, not forty five. So no vertical solution.
<excited>Both genuine slopes come from the algebra: minus two, or one half.</excited> Miss either the plus-or-minus or the vertical check and you lose marks.
Let's close the subtopic by locking in the four traps that eat marks on slope questions.
Trap one, the biggest of all: a vertical line's slope is undefined. Not infinity, not zero. Zero is the horizontal line; mixing these two poles is the single most common slope error.
Trap two: perpendicular means the product of slopes is minus one, not plus one. If both your perpendicular slopes share a sign, you have already made the mistake.

Trap three: when a problem asks for the line making a given angle with another, set the signed ratio equal to plus or minus tan of that angle, because there are genuinely two such lines. Use the modulus only when you want the angle between two given lines.
Trap four: the moment you write 'let the slope be m', you have quietly excluded vertical lines. In Advanced problems, check the vertical case on its own.
<whisper>And the pro-tip: before any computation, just look at the picture. Rising means positive, falling means negative, flat means zero, upright means undefined.</whisper>
That two-second sign check catches most arithmetic slips before they ever cost you a mark.
Slope is the workhorse of this entire chapter, so keep those two poles — horizontal zero, vertical undefined — crystal clear.
<curious>Why does one simple line need six different equations?</curious> Let's see what each one is really for.
A line is the simplest curve there is, and yet it can appear in six different costumes.
Each costume answers a different clue you are handed: sometimes a point and a direction, sometimes two points, sometimes where it crosses the axes, sometimes how far it sits from the origin.
Picture one single line, labelled every way at once: a point on it, its two axis crossings, and the perpendicular from the origin. Every description pins down the same line.
All six are really dialects of one sentence, the general form A x plus B y plus C equals zero. Any line at all can be written this way.
Two cautions. The slope-intercept and point-slope forms both assume a slope exists, so neither can describe a vertical line.
And intercept form falls apart when the line passes through the origin, or runs parallel to an axis, because an intercept goes missing or to zero.

So the skill that actually earns marks is not memorising six formulas; it is translating between them on demand — pull the slope out of the general form, or rewrite point-slope as intercept form in seconds.
Here is the beautiful part: five of the six forms descend from one tiny proof. Let's build it.
Take a line of slope m through a fixed point x one, y one, and let x, y be any other point sitting on it.
The slope you would compute from those two points has to equal the line's own slope m — that is what being on the line means.
So y minus y one over x minus x one equals m.
Multiply across and you get y minus y one equals m times x minus x one. That is the point-slope form, and everything else grows from it.
Need the two-point form? Just replace the slope m by the two-point slope, y two minus y one over x two minus x one.
That gives y minus y one equals that fraction times x minus x one — the same proof, one substitution later.
And if the fixed point happens to be zero comma c, the equation collapses straight to y equals m x plus c, the slope-intercept form. One proof, three forms.
Now the two forms built from special clues — intercept form and normal form.
For intercept form, feed the two axis crossings, a comma zero and zero comma b, into the two-point form.
The slope between them is b minus zero over zero minus a, so y equals minus b over a, times x minus a.
Multiply out and divide by b, and it tidies into x over a plus y over b equals one — clean and symmetric.
Geometrically it is just the line closing off a right triangle with the two axes, cutting them at a and at b.
The normal form uses a different clue: the perpendicular distance p from the origin, at angle omega. The foot of that perpendicular sits at p cos omega, p sin omega.
Picture the perpendicular O N of length p, tilted at angle omega. The line we want passes through N, at right angles to O N.
Write the line through N with the right perpendicular slope, multiply through by sin omega, and use the identity cos squared plus sin squared equals one.
Everything collapses to x cos omega plus y sin omega equals p — the normal form, with p as the honest distance from the origin.
This one step trips up more students than any other in the subtopic, so let's walk it slowly.
Start with the general form and move the constant to the right: A x plus B y equals minus C.
Now divide both sides by the square root of A squared plus B squared — but with a sign in front, chosen so the right-hand side comes out positive.
Why the sign choice? Because that right side becomes p, and p is a distance, which can never be negative. Concretely, pick the sign opposite to the sign of C.
Once divided, cos omega is A over the signed root, and sin omega is B over the same signed root.
And p is simply the modulus of C over the root of A squared plus B squared.
The last trap: find omega from the signs of cos omega and sin omega together, because those two fix the quadrant. Reading it from cos omega alone leaves you guessing between two angles.
And remember, whatever the situation, the general form never fails — it is the one description that always works, so keep it as your fallback.

board_events.text: Worked: Two-Point & General Form
Example 1: line through $(-2,5)$ and $(3,-1)$; find it and its $y$-intercept.
Example 2: for $3x - 4y + 12 = 0$, read the slope and intercepts fast.
Slope is $-\tfrac{A}{B}$, not $\tfrac{A}{B}$ — the sign trap.
Worked: Perpendicular Line, Intercept Form
Line through $(2,3)$ perpendicular to $4x - 3y + 7 = 0$; give intercept form.
Now divide $3x + 4y = 18$ by $18$ for intercept form.
Chain: reduction gives slope, flip-and-negate gives $\perp$, then convert form.
Worked: Normal Form (Advanced)
Reduce $x - \sqrt{3}\,y + 8 = 0$ to normal form; find $p$ and $\omega$.
Since $C = 8 > 0$, divide by $-2$ so the right side becomes positive.
$\cos\omega < 0$ and $\sin\omega > 0$ place $\omega$ in the second quadrant: $\omega = 120^\circ$.
Dividing by $+2$ instead would give '$p = -4$' — a forbidden negative distance.
Pitfalls: Equations of a Line
Slope from the general form is $m = -\tfrac{A}{B}$, not $\tfrac{A}{B}$.
A negative $p$ in normal form means the wrong sign was chosen — flip it.
Read $\omega$ from the signs of both $\cos\omega$ and $\sin\omega$, never one alone.
Lines through the origin or parallel to an axis have no valid intercept form.
Pro-tip: set $y=0$ for the $x$-intercept and $x=0$ for the $y$-intercept — no signs to memorise.
The substitution carries the signs for you, every time.
And the general form never fails — keep it as your universal fallback.
Distance = the Perpendicular Drop
The distance from a point to a line is the shortest path — the perpendicular dropped onto it.
The vector $(A,B)$ points perpendicular to $Ax + By + C = 0$: its normal direction.

board_events.text: Two parallel lines share one normal, so their distance collapses to a constant.
The symmetric form describes a line as 'stand at $P$, face $\theta$, walk a distance $r$'.
All three tools give the perpendicular distance — never a slant along some other direction.
Proof: Distance of a Point from a Line
Every first-degree equation $Ax+By+C=0$ is a line: rewrite it as $y = -\tfrac{A}{B}x - \tfrac{C}{B}$ or as $x = -\tfrac{C}{A}$.
The unit normal is $\hat{n} = \dfrac{(A,B)}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2}}$; pick any point $R(x_0,y_0)$ on the line.
The distance is the projection of $\vec{RP}$ onto $\hat{n}$.
The signed value, without the bars, tells you which side of the line $P$ lies on.

segments.text: Two quick examples: build a line from two points, then dissect one already in general form.
Example one: find the line through minus two, five and three, minus one, and give its y-intercept.
Slope first: minus one minus five over three minus minus two, which is minus six over five.
Point-slope through minus two, five, then clear fractions, and you land on six x plus five y minus thirteen equals zero. Setting x to zero gives the y-intercept, thirteen over five.
Example two: for three x minus four y plus twelve equals zero, read everything off with the reduction formulas.
Slope is minus A over B, that is minus three over minus four, which is plus three over four.
For the intercepts, set y to zero to get x equals minus four, and set x to zero to get y equals three.

The trap lives right here: the slope is minus A over B, not A over B. Both plus and minus three over four appear on the option list, so anchor it — the line rises to the right, so the slope is positive.
This example chains three ideas: reading a slope, building a perpendicular, and converting to intercept form.
We want the line through two, three that is perpendicular to four x minus three y plus seven equals zero, expressed in intercept form.
First read the given line's slope by reduction: minus A over B is minus four over minus three, that is four over three.
Perpendicular means flip and negate, so our slope is minus three over four.
Point-slope through two, three, then clear fractions, gives three x plus four y minus eighteen equals zero.
For intercept form, write three x plus four y equals eighteen, and divide the whole thing by eighteen.
That gives x over six plus y over nine-halves equals one — so the x-intercept is six and the y-intercept is four point five.
Notice the chain: the reduction formula handed us a slope, flip-and-negate gave the perpendicular, and one division converted the form. Three subtopic ideas, one clean problem.
<curious>Now the Advanced version, where the sign choice is the whole game.</curious>
Reduce x minus root three y plus eight equals zero to normal form, and find both p and omega exactly.
Here A is one, B is minus root three, so the root of A squared plus B squared is the root of one plus three, which is two.
The constant C is plus eight, which is positive, so we must divide by minus two to force the right-hand side positive.
Dividing gives minus one half x plus root three over two y equals four.
So cos omega is minus one half, sin omega is root three over two, and p is four.
Now read omega from both signs together: cosine negative and sine positive put omega in the second quadrant, so omega is one hundred twenty degrees.
Had we divided by plus two instead, the right side would read minus four, claiming p equals minus four — a negative distance, which is forbidden. That alone flags the wrong sign choice.
So the normal form is x cos one hundred twenty plus y sin one hundred twenty equals four, with p four and omega one hundred twenty degrees.
Let's close this subtopic with the four traps examiners plant in equation problems.
Trap one, the most frequent: the slope from the general form is minus A over B, not A over B. Forgetting that minus is the classic error.
Trap two: if your normal-form reduction ever hands you a negative p, you chose the wrong sign for the radical. A distance cannot be negative, so just flip it.
Trap three: fix omega from the signs of both cosine and sine together. Cosine alone leaves one hundred twenty and two hundred forty degrees indistinguishable.
Trap four: do not force intercept form onto a line through the origin or one parallel to an axis — it has no valid intercept form there.
<whisper>And the pro-tip that saves sign errors: to find intercepts, just set y to zero for the x-intercept and x to zero for the y-intercept.</whisper>
The substitution carries all the signs for you, so you never have to recall minus C over A or minus C over B under pressure.
And whenever a form feels awkward, fall back on the general form — it is the one description that never fails.
You can already write a line; the natural next question is how far something is from it.
If a railway track is the line and your house is a point, the distance that matters is not some random diagonal — it is the shortest path, the perpendicular dropped straight onto the track.
Here is the quiet fact that powers everything: the vector A comma B points perpendicular to the line A x plus B y plus C equals zero. That is the line's normal direction.
So to measure how far a point P sits from the line, you just project the gap between P and the line onto that normal direction and read off the length.
That projection is exactly the famous formula: d equals the modulus of A x one plus B y one plus C, over the root of A squared plus B squared.
Two parallel lines are just a special case: they share the same normal, so the distance between them collapses to one clean constant.
There is also a third tool, the symmetric form, which describes a line as: stand at P, face the inclination theta, and walk a signed distance r.
One thing ties them together: all three measure the perpendicular distance, never a slant along some arbitrary direction.
Let's derive the point-to-line formula so it becomes something you can rebuild, not just recall.

First a quick lead-in: every first-degree equation is genuinely a line. If B is non-zero, rewrite it as y equals minus A over B, x, minus C over B; if B is zero, it is the vertical line x equals minus C over A.
Now the unit normal is the vector A comma B divided by the root of A squared plus B squared. Pick any point R on the line at all.
Since R lies on the line, A x nought plus B y nought plus C equals zero, so A x nought plus B y nought equals minus C. Hold that.
The perpendicular distance from P is just the length of the projection of the vector from R to P onto the unit normal.
That projection is the modulus of A times x one minus x nought, plus B times y one minus y nought, all over the root.
Substitute the fact we held: the bracket becomes A x one plus B y one plus C, and the distance is the modulus of that over the root of A squared plus B squared.
One bonus: keep the signed value without the bars and its sign tells you which side of the line P is on — a fact we will exploit later.

board_events.text: Proof: Parallel Lines & the Symmetric Form
Parallel lines $Ax+By+C_1=0$ and $Ax+By+C_2=0$ are everywhere the same distance apart.
Pick the point $\left(-\tfrac{C_1}{A},\, 0\right)$ on the first, then measure to the second.
Valid only after both lines show identical $A$ and $B$ — normalize first.

Worked: Point-Line & Parallel Lines
Example 1: distance of $(3,-4)$ from $4x + 3y - 5 = 0$.

Find the perpendicular distance from the origin to the line joining $A(1,2)$ and $B(4,6)$.
Now apply the point-line distance from $O(0,0)$.
Two subtopics chained: the two-point equation, then the distance formula.
The answer is two-fifths, or zero point four units.

A line through $P(1,1)$ with $\theta = 60^\circ$ meets $2x + y = 8$ at $Q$. Find $PQ$.

Two non-parallel roads cross at exactly one junction.

board_events.text: Three lines through one point are concurrent — a very common exam setup.
You could intersect two and test the third, but a determinant does it in one shot.
A unique intersection needs non-parallel lines: $a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1 \ne 0$.
Parallel lines never meet; coincident lines meet everywhere.
The Family Trick: $L_1 + \lambda L_2 = 0$
Suppose $L_1 = 0$ and $L_2 = 0$ cross at a junction $J$.

board_events.text: At $J$, both $L_1$ and $L_2$ are zero, so the combination is automatically zero too.
So this is a whole family of lines through $J$ — one line for each value of $\lambda$.
The family captures every line through $J$ except $L_2 = 0$ itself (that needs $\lambda \to \infty$).
Impose one extra condition to pin down $\lambda$ — you never compute $J$ at all.

segments.text: Now two shorter derivations: the gap between parallel lines, and why the symmetric form hands you distance for free.
Two parallel lines share the same A and B and differ only in the constant. Since they are parallel, they sit the same distance apart everywhere.
So the trick is easy: grab a convenient point on the first line, say minus C one over A comma zero, and measure its distance to the second line with the formula we just proved.
The A x and B y terms cancel neatly, and what survives is the modulus of C one minus C two over the root of A squared plus B squared.
One firm condition, though: this only works once both lines show identical A and B. If they do not, normalize one line first, or your answer is simply wrong.
Now the symmetric form. Start at P, face the inclination theta, and step a signed distance r along that direction.
The point you reach has coordinates x one plus r cos theta, and y one plus r sin theta.
And here is the elegance: because cos theta, sin theta is a unit step, the parameter r is the genuine distance travelled — so solving for r reads off distances directly.
Two worked examples: a plain point-to-line distance, then a parallel-line trap.
Example one: the distance of the point three, minus four from the line four x plus three y minus five equals zero.
Plug in: four times three plus three times minus four minus five, in modulus, is five; the root of sixteen plus nine is five; so the distance is one unit.
Example two: the distance between three x minus four y plus seven equals zero and six x minus eight y minus five equals zero.
The lines are parallel, but not yet comparable — the second has doubled coefficients. Divide it by two to get three x minus four y minus two point five equals zero.
Now C one is seven and C two is minus two point five, over the root, which is five. The distance is nine point five over five, that is one point nine.
The trap is using the lines as written: modulus of seven minus minus five over five gives two point four — exactly the planted wrong answer.
So the rule is absolute: always normalize both lines to identical A and B before you subtract the constants.
This example chains the two-point equation from the last subtopic into the distance formula from this one.
Find the perpendicular distance from the origin to the line joining A at one, two and B at four, six.
Step one is the line's equation. Its slope is six minus two over four minus one, which is four over three.
Point-slope through one, two, cleared of fractions, gives four x minus three y plus two equals zero.
Step two: apply the point-to-line distance, using the origin at zero, zero as the point.
That is the modulus of four times zero minus three times zero plus two, over the root of sixteen plus nine, which is two over five.
Notice the two-subtopic chain: first you built the line from two points, then you measured with the distance formula. No shortcut skips the equation step.
So the answer is two-fifths, or zero point four units. Clean and direct.
<excited>Here is where the symmetric form really shines — it delivers a distance as a single solved number.</excited>
A line through P at one, one with inclination sixty degrees meets the line two x plus y equals eight at Q. Find the length P Q.
Parametrize with the unit direction cos sixty, sin sixty, which is one half and root three over two. So x is one plus r over two, and y is one plus root three over two, r.
Now substitute both into two x plus y equals eight and solve straight for r — and that r is the distance we want.
The substitution gives two times the quantity one plus r over two, plus the quantity one plus root three over two r, equals eight.
That simplifies to r times one plus root three over two equals five, so r equals ten over two plus root three.
Rationalize the denominator and r becomes ten times two minus root three, that is twenty minus ten root three, about two point six eight units.
The whole trick rests on using the unit direction. Feed in non-unit direction numbers and the parameter stops equalling the true length — that failure is silent, so guard against it.
Let's talk about where lines meet — one of the most heavily tested ideas in the whole chapter.
Two roads that are not parallel cross at exactly one junction. There is one meeting point, no more.
Finding that junction algebraically is nothing fancy: it is just solving the two line equations together, the pair of x and y that satisfies both.
Now scale up. When do three roads all meet at a single roundabout? Look at the picture — three lines threading one common point.
That situation is called concurrency, and it appears again and again, in medians meeting, altitudes meeting, and so on.
You could find where two of them cross and then check the third passes through it — but there is a slicker determinant test that settles it in a single computation.
One caution: a unique intersection only exists when the lines are not parallel, which the algebra encodes as a one b two minus a two b one, not equal to zero.
If that quantity is zero, the lines are either parallel and never meet, or coincident and meet everywhere.
<curious>Here is the cleverest single idea in the whole chapter — and it feels like magic the first time.</curious>
Suppose two lines, L one equals zero and L two equals zero, cross at some junction J.
Now watch the picture: every one of these dashed lines passes through J too. What are they?
Consider the combination L one plus lambda times L two. At the junction J, both L one and L two are exactly zero, so the whole combination is automatically zero there, whatever lambda is.
In symbols, L one plus lambda L two equals zero.
So this single expression is a whole family of lines, all passing through J, one line for each value of lambda you choose.
One fine print: this family reaches every line through J except L two itself, which would need lambda running off to infinity. If your answer might be L two, check it on its own.
And the payoff: if you need the line through J that also meets one more condition, just impose that condition to fix lambda — you never have to find J at all.

board_events.text: Proof: The Family Passes Through $J$
Let $L_1 \equiv a_1 x + b_1 y + c_1$ and $L_2 \equiv a_2 x + b_2 y + c_2$ meet at $J(x_0, y_0)$.
Since $J$ lies on both lines, each expression vanishes there.
So $J$ satisfies $L_1 + \lambda L_2 = 0$ for every $\lambda$.
And $L_1 + \lambda L_2 = 0$ is first-degree, so it is itself a line through $J$.
'Both zero $\Rightarrow$ sum zero' — that is the whole reason the trick works.
Proof: The Concurrency Determinant
Three lines $L_i \equiv a_i x + b_i y + c_i = 0$, with no two parallel.
Let $L_1, L_2$ meet at $J(x_0, y_0)$; concurrency means $L_3$ also passes through $J$.

board_events.text: This homogeneous system has the nonzero solution $(x_0, y_0, 1)$.
A homogeneous system has a nonzero solution only if its determinant vanishes.

segments.text: Let's prove that the family really does pass through the junction — it is a two-line argument.
Write L one as a one x plus b one y plus c one, and L two as a two x plus b two y plus c two, meeting at the junction J with coordinates x nought, y nought.
Because J sits on both lines, each of these expressions evaluates to zero when you plug in J.
That is, L one at J is zero, and L two at J is zero.
Now form the combination at J: L one at J plus lambda times L two at J is zero plus lambda times zero, which is zero.
So J satisfies L one plus lambda L two equals zero for every single value of lambda — the junction is on all of them.
And since L one plus lambda L two is still a first-degree expression, its graph is a line, so it is genuinely a line through J.
The entire trick rests on that one clean fact: both zero implies the sum is zero. That is why the junction rides along for free.
Now the determinant test for concurrency, and why it works.
Take three lines, L one, L two, L three, in general form, and assume no two of them are parallel.
Let the first two meet at the junction J. Concurrency simply means the third line also passes through that same J.
So all three equations hold at J. Stack them as a matrix of coefficients times the column x nought, y nought, one, and the result is the zero vector.
That is a homogeneous system, and it has a genuinely nonzero solution, namely x nought, y nought, one — the last entry is one, so it cannot be all zeros.
Here is the key algebra fact: a homogeneous system can have a nonzero solution only if its coefficient determinant is zero.
So concurrency forces that three by three determinant of the coefficients to vanish. That is the whole test.
And the family procedure in practice: write L one plus lambda L two equals zero, impose whatever extra condition the problem gives, and solve for lambda.
If it must pass through a point, substitute the point; if it has a given slope, set minus A over B equal to it; if it is perpendicular to something, set the slope product to minus one.
Two examples: a plain intersection, then a concurrency check by determinant.
Example one: find where two x plus three y minus eight equals zero meets x minus y plus one equals zero.
From the second line, x equals y minus one. Substitute into the first: two times y minus one, plus three y minus eight, equals zero, which gives five y equals ten.
So y is two and x is one; the intersection is the point one comma two.
Example two: are the three lines x plus y minus two, two x minus y minus one, and four x minus y minus five all concurrent?
Drop straight into the determinant — do not solve two and test the third. Expanding along the top row gives four, minus a negative six, minus four, which is six.
The determinant is six, which is not zero, so the three lines are not concurrent.
The only trap here is a sign slip in the cofactor expansion, so anchor the plus, minus, plus pattern across the top row and expand slowly.
<excited>Now the family method in action — watch us solve without ever finding the intersection.</excited>
Find the line through the intersection of x plus two y minus five and three x minus y plus one that also passes through the point two comma one.
Write the family: the quantity x plus two y minus five, plus lambda times the quantity three x minus y plus one, equals zero.
Now impose the extra condition that it passes through two comma one — just substitute those coordinates.
That gives two plus two minus five, plus lambda times six minus one plus one, equals zero, which is minus one plus six lambda equals zero.
So lambda is one sixth.
Substitute lambda back, clear the fraction, and you get nine x plus eleven y minus twenty nine equals zero.
And notice the whole point: we never computed the intersection of the two lines. Skipping that step is exactly the elegance examiners reward.
<curious>An Advanced twist: solving the determinant is only half the job — the parallel-check is the trap.</curious>
For what value of a are the lines a x plus two y plus one, two x plus a y plus two, and x plus y minus one all concurrent?
Set the coefficient determinant to zero.
Expanding along the top row: a times minus a minus two, minus two times minus two minus two, plus the quantity two minus a. That collapses to minus a squared minus three a plus ten equals zero.
Multiply through by minus one: a squared plus three a minus ten equals zero, which factors as a plus five, times a minus two.
So a is minus five or a is two — two candidates from the algebra.

Now the Advanced check. At a equals two, the first two lines become two x plus two y plus one and two x plus two y plus two — parallel and distinct, so they never meet, and concurrency is impossible. Discard a equals two.
At a equals minus five, no two lines are parallel, so it survives. The single valid answer is a equals minus five.

segments.text: Let's close this subtopic with the traps and the one habit that saves the most time.
Trap one, really a time-saver: if a question wants a line through an intersection plus one more condition, reach for L one plus lambda L two equals zero and skip finding the point entirely.
Trap two: a zero concurrency determinant can also be satisfied by a degenerate, parallel configuration, so always verify that no two of the lines are parallel.
Trap three: the family L one plus lambda L two can produce every line through the junction except L two itself. If L two might be your answer, test that case on its own.
Trap four: when expanding a three by three determinant, keep the plus, minus, plus sign pattern explicit across your chosen row — rushing the middle term is where marks vanish.
<whisper>And the pro-tip: the phrase 'line through the intersection of, and' should trigger the family trick instantly, before you write anything else.</whisper>
Finding the intersection point first is almost always the slower path, and it introduces extra arithmetic to slip on.
Sum it up as: determinant dies, they meet — always with the no-two-parallel caveat attached.
When two lines cross, they make four angles in two equal pairs, and the bisectors are the lines that split those angles exactly in half.
Look at the picture: two crossing lines, and their two bisectors. Notice something — the bisectors sit at right angles to each other, always.
Because they bisect supplementary angles, once you have one bisector, the other is automatically perpendicular to it.
The defining property is beautifully simple: a point lies on a bisector exactly when it is the same perpendicular distance from both lines. Equidistant means on the bisector.
Since distance from a line is that familiar expression over the root of a squared plus b squared, equidistant becomes the first ratio equal to plus or minus the second.
Dropping the two moduli is what introduces the plus or minus, and that single sign choice is the whole story: the two signs give the two bisectors.
One crucial setup: the clean identification rules only work if you first rewrite both lines with positive constant terms. Skip that and every sign rule inverts on you.
And keep in mind the free check: whatever two bisectors you compute, they must come out perpendicular.
Let's prove that the bisector really is the locus of equidistant points — it follows straight from the distance formula.
Take a point P that is equidistant from the two lines L one and L two.
Picture it: the perpendicular from P to the first line and the perpendicular to the second are the same length.
Write that as an equation using the point-to-line distance: the modulus of L one over its own root equals the modulus of L two over its own root.
Now remove the moduli. Two expressions can have equal absolute values in exactly two ways — they are equal, or they are negatives of each other.
That is exactly the plus or minus: the first ratio equals plus or minus the second.
Each choice of sign is a first-degree equation, so each is a line. Together, those two lines are the two angle bisectors.
One thing students routinely botch: each line carries its own denominator, the root of its own a squared plus b squared. Never share a single denominator across both.
Writing the two bisectors is easy; the real exam skill is telling which is which. Here is the procedure.
Step one: rewrite both lines so their constant terms are positive. If a constant is negative, multiply that whole equation by minus one.
Step two: with both constants positive, the plus sign always gives the bisector of the angle that contains the origin.

Why does forcing positive constants matter? Because the sign of the constant encodes which side of the line the origin is on; making both positive pins the origin to the positive side of both, and that is what makes the plus sign mean the origin's angle.
Step three: to label acute versus obtuse, compute a one a two plus b one b two, using the positive-constant forms.
If that sum is positive, the plus bisector is the obtuse one.
If that sum is negative, the plus bisector is the acute one.
And whatever you get, the two bisectors must satisfy m one times m two equals minus one — verify that perpendicularity at the end as a check.
Two examples: first write both bisectors, then pick out just the origin's bisector.
Example one: the bisectors of three x minus four y plus seven and five x plus twelve y minus two.
The roots are five and thirteen, so set three x minus four y plus seven over five equal to plus or minus five x plus twelve y minus two over thirteen.
Take the plus sign, cross-multiply, and simplify to fourteen x minus one hundred twelve y plus one hundred one equals zero.
Take the minus sign and you get sixty four x plus eight y plus eighty one equals zero. Those are the two bisectors.
Example two: find only the bisector of the angle containing the origin for four x plus three y minus six and five x plus twelve y plus nine.
First make constants positive. The first has a negative six, so multiply it by minus one to get minus four x minus three y plus six. The second already has plus nine.
Now take the plus sign: minus four x minus three y plus six over five equals five x plus twelve y plus nine over thirteen.
Cross-multiply and simplify, and the origin's bisector is seven x plus nine y minus three equals zero.

board_events.text: Worked: Identifying the Acute Bisector
For $x + y - 2 = 0$ and $7x - y + 3 = 0$, find the acute-angle bisector.
Make constants positive: rewrite the first as $-x - y + 2 = 0$.
With positive constants and $a_1 a_2 + b_1 b_2 < 0$, the '+' sign is the acute bisector.
Normalize constants first, then read the acute/obtuse rule — order matters.
Worked: Bisectors Are Perpendicular (Advanced)
Verify perpendicularity for the two bisectors found in Example 1.
Why it must hold: the bisectors split supplementary angles, differing by exactly $90^\circ$.
If one angle is $2\alpha$, the other is $2(90^\circ - \alpha)$ — half-lines $90^\circ$ apart.
So this perpendicularity is a structural fact, and a free sanity check every time.
Pitfalls: Angle Bisectors
Skipping the positive-constant normalization inverts every identification rule.
Acute/obtuse rule: with $c_1, c_2 > 0$, $a_1 a_2 + b_1 b_2 > 0 \Rightarrow$ '+' obtuse; $< 0 \Rightarrow$ '+' acute.
Your two bisectors must satisfy $m_1 m_2 = -1$; if not, there is an arithmetic error.
Each line gets its own $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ — do not share one denominator.
Pro-tip: the origin's bisector is the '+' one after making constants positive — memorise that anchor.
Compute $a_1 a_2 + b_1 b_2$ only when the question actually asks acute versus obtuse.
Don't compute everything — compute exactly what's asked.
Foot, Image & Reflection

segments.text: Now the harder skill: not just writing a bisector, but identifying the acute one.
For x plus y minus two and seven x minus y plus three, find the acute-angle bisector.
First make constants positive. The first line has a negative constant, so rewrite it as minus x minus y plus two. The second already has plus three.
Now compute a one a two plus b one b two with these forms: minus one times seven, plus minus one times minus one, which is minus seven plus one, that is minus six.
Since the constants are positive and this sum is negative, the rule tells us the plus sign gives the acute bisector.
So take the plus sign: minus x minus y plus two over root two equals seven x minus y plus three over root fifty.
Since root fifty is five root two, multiply both sides by five root two and simplify, giving twelve x plus four y minus seven equals zero — the acute-angle bisector.
The order is everything here: normalize the constants first, then read the acute-obtuse rule. Reverse them and the rule points the wrong way.
This Advanced example confirms the free check we keep mentioning — that the two bisectors are perpendicular.
Take the two bisectors we found in example one and verify their slopes multiply to minus one.
The first bisector, fourteen x minus one hundred twelve y plus one hundred one, has slope fourteen over one hundred twelve, which is one eighth.
The second, sixty four x plus eight y plus eighty one, has slope minus sixty four over eight, which is minus eight.
Their product is one eighth times minus eight, which is minus one — perpendicular, confirmed.
Now why it must always hold: the two bisectors split the two supplementary angles at the crossing, and those half-lines differ in direction by exactly ninety degrees.
If one full angle is two alpha, the other is two times ninety minus alpha, so their bisecting directions sit exactly ninety degrees apart.
So the perpendicularity is not a coincidence, it is structural — which makes it a free sanity check on every bisector computation you ever do.
Let's close bisectors with the traps and one clean anchor to memorise.
Trap one, the biggest: skipping the positive-constant normalization. Every identification rule — origin, acute, obtuse — assumes both constants are positive, so normalize first, every single time.

Trap two: get the acute-obtuse direction right. With positive constants, a one a two plus b one b two positive means the plus bisector is obtuse; negative means it is acute. Write it down before deciding.
Trap three: your two bisectors must satisfy slope one times slope two equals minus one. If they do not, you have an arithmetic error somewhere — go back.
Trap four: each line gets its own root of a squared plus b squared. Do not share a single denominator across the two lines.

Only reach for a one a two plus b one b two when the question specifically asks acute versus obtuse.
In short, do not compute everything — compute exactly what is asked, and no more.
This last subtopic is really one picture, turned into formulas. Let's set the picture up.

Stand at a point P and shine a torch straight at a wall, and let the wall be our line. The spot where the beam hits perpendicularly is the foot of the perpendicular — the closest point on the line to P.
Look at the diagram: P above the line, the foot Q on the line, and the image P-prime on the far side. Notice Q sits exactly halfway between P and P-prime.
Now walk an equal distance past the wall along that same beam, and you reach the image — exactly as far behind the mirror as you stand in front, just like your reflection in glass.
So two facts fall out at once: the foot is halfway to the image, and the image is twice as far as the foot.
How do we get there algebraically? The line has normal direction a comma b, and you step from P straight along that normal until you land on the line.
The size of that step is governed by a x one plus b y one plus c, over a squared plus b squared — the very expression that measured distance earlier, now reused as a step size.
And the whole subtopic is just: take one step to reach the foot, and two steps to reach the mirror image.
Let's derive the foot formula — it is a single clean idea about stepping along the normal.
The segment from P to the foot Q is perpendicular to the line, which means it points exactly along the line's normal direction, a comma b.
So Q is reached from P by stepping some scalar amount t along that normal, as the diagram shows.
That is, Q equals x one plus t a, and y one plus t b.
But Q also lies on the line, so plug those coordinates into the line's equation and solve for the one unknown t.
Substituting gives a times x one plus t a, plus b times y one plus t b, plus c, equals zero.
Grouping the t terms and rearranging, t comes out as minus a x one plus b y one plus c, over a squared plus b squared.
Feed that t back in, and the foot satisfies x minus x one over a, equals y minus y one over b, equals that same step — the compact foot formula.

board_events.text: Proof: Image of a Point, Reflecting a Line
The foot $Q$ is the midpoint of $P$ and its image $P'$, so $P' = 2Q - P$.
So the image uses parameter $2t$ — exactly double the foot's step.
To reflect a whole line $m$ in a line $\ell$: reflect two of its points and rejoin them.
Shortcut: if $m$ and $\ell$ intersect, the reflection also passes through $m \cap \ell$.
So one image point plus that intersection is enough — half the work.
Worked: Foot & Image in $y = x$
Example 1: foot of the perpendicular from $P(2,3)$ to $x + y - 1 = 0$.
Example 2: image of $(4,-1)$ in the line $y = x$.
$y = x$ is a special mirror — just swap the coordinates.
Recognise $y=x$, the $x$-axis, and the $y$-axis on sight, and use swap or negate.
Worked: Image & Verifying Equal Distances
Find the image of $P(1,1)$ in the line $3x - 4y + 5 = 0$.
Distance of $P$ from the line is $\tfrac{|4|}{5} = 0.8$.
Equal distances, opposite sides — exactly what a mirror image must satisfy.
Worked: Reflected Ray (Advanced)
A ray along $x - 2y + 5 = 0$ strikes the mirror $3x - 4y + 4 = 0$. Find the reflected ray.
Incidence point $I$: solve the two lines together.
Take $A(-5,0)$ on the incident ray and reflect it in the mirror.
Pitfalls: Foot, Image & Reflection
Foot uses the step $-\tfrac{ax_1+by_1+c}{a^2+b^2}$; the image uses twice that — do not drop the $2$.
For $y=x$, the $x$-axis, and the $y$-axis, use swap or negate — faster and error-proof.
You cannot reflect an equation directly (except in $y=x$); reflect points instead.
Denominator here is $a^2+b^2$, no root — contrast with the distance formula's $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.
Pro-tip: reflecting a line? One image point plus the mirror intersection is enough.
That halves the work versus reflecting two separate points.
One step to the foot, two steps to the mirror — keep the factor of two straight.

segments.text: Now the image formula, which follows from the foot in one step, plus how to reflect a whole line.
The foot Q is the midpoint of P and its image P-prime. So P-prime equals two Q minus P — just the midpoint relation rearranged.
Substitute Q as P plus t times a comma b, and P-prime becomes P plus two t times a comma b.
So the image uses the parameter two t, exactly double the foot's step. That is the only change from the foot formula.
In coordinates, x-prime minus x one over a equals y-prime minus y one over b equals minus two times a x one plus b y one plus c, over a squared plus b squared.
To reflect a whole line m in a mirror line ell, you cannot tweak the equation directly — instead reflect two of its points and join the images.
There is a neat shortcut: if m and the mirror ell actually intersect, the reflected line also passes through their point of intersection.
So one image point, plus that intersection, is enough to fix the reflected line — which halves the work versus reflecting two separate points.
Two examples: a foot by the general formula, then an image by the fast special-mirror trick.
Example one: find the foot of the perpendicular from P at two, three to the line x plus y minus one equals zero.
Here a and b are both one, and c is minus one. So a x one plus b y one plus c is two plus three minus one, that is four; a squared plus b squared is two; so the step t is minus two.
Then Q is two plus t times one, and three plus t times one, which is zero comma one — the foot.
Example two: find the image of four comma minus one in the line y equals x.
Do not grind the general formula here — y equals x is a special mirror, so you simply swap the two coordinates.
Swapping gives minus one comma four. Done in one move.
So train your eye: the moment you see y equals x, the x-axis, or the y-axis, reach for swap or negate rather than the full machinery.
This example finds an image and then checks it, so you learn to trust your own answer.
Find the image of P at one, one in the line three x minus four y plus five equals zero.
Compute a x one plus b y one plus c: three minus four plus five, which is four; and a squared plus b squared is twenty five.
The image step is minus two times four over twenty five, that is minus eight over twenty five.
So P-prime is one minus twenty four over twenty five, and one plus thirty two over twenty five, which is one over twenty five, comma fifty seven over twenty five.
Now verify. The distance of P from the line is the modulus of four over five, that is zero point eight.
Plug P-prime into the distance formula and it also comes out to four over five, zero point eight.
Equal distances on opposite sides of the line — which is exactly the defining property of a mirror image. The check confirms the answer.
<curious>Here is the Advanced payoff — reflection turns an optics problem into two coordinate computations.</curious>
A ray of light travelling along x minus two y plus five equals zero strikes the mirror three x minus four y plus four equals zero. Find the reflected ray.
The reflected ray passes through the incidence point, so first find where the incident ray meets the mirror by solving the two lines together.
That intersection is the point I, at six comma eleven halves.
Now take any convenient point on the incident ray — say A at minus five, zero — and reflect it in the mirror using the image formula.
Here a A x plus b A y plus c is minus fifteen plus four, that is minus eleven, and the image step works out to twenty two over twenty five.
That sends A to its image A-prime, at minus fifty nine over twenty five, comma minus eighty eight over twenty five.

The reflected ray is simply the line joining I and A-prime, and working out its equation gives forty one x minus thirty eight y minus thirty seven equals zero. Two coordinate steps, and the optics is done.
Let's close the last subtopic with its four traps.
Trap one: the foot uses the single step, but the image uses twice that step. Drop the factor of two and you land right on the line instead of behind it.
Trap two: for the special mirrors — y equals x, the x-axis, and the y-axis — use swap or negate. It is faster and essentially error-proof.
Trap three: you cannot reflect an equation by tweaking its coefficients, except for the y equals x case where swapping x and y works. In general, reflect points instead.
Trap four: the denominator in these formulas is a squared plus b squared, with no square root, which contrasts with the distance formula's root of a squared plus b squared. Mixing them is common.

This example finds an image and then checks it, so you learn to trust your own answer.

segments.text: Let's actually prove the section formula, because a formula you can rebuild is a formula you never forget.
Take points A and B, and let P divide the segment internally in the ratio m to n. Now drop perpendiculars from all three points straight down to the x-axis.
Those perpendiculars carve out two similar right triangles, one sitting inside the other.
Because the triangles are similar, the way P splits the segment in the ratio m to n is copied exactly onto the x-coordinates along the base.
So the ratio of x P minus x one to x two minus x P equals m over n.
Cross-multiply and gather the x P terms: n times the first bracket equals m times the second, which rearranges to x P times m plus n equals m x two plus n x one.
Divide through by m plus n and x P pops out as m x two plus n x one, all over m plus n.
<excited>The y-coordinate follows by the identical argument, giving the full section point.</excited> Notice the denominator is m plus n for internal division — hold onto that.
Here is your complete toolkit for points — keep this board as your reference.
Distance: A B equals the square root of x two minus x one, squared, plus y two minus y one, squared. It is just Pythagoras on the plane.
Internal section point in the ratio m to n uses the denominator m plus n, with the coordinates cross-weighted as shown.
The external version is nearly identical, but every plus becomes a minus — denominator m minus n.
The midpoint is simply the internal formula at ratio one to one: average the x-coordinates, average the y-coordinates.
The centroid of a triangle averages all three vertices, dividing each sum by three.
The area is one half the modulus of that cyclic expression in x and y.
And the single most useful consequence: the area is zero exactly when the three points are collinear.
Finally, to shift the origin to the point h comma k, the new coordinates are old minus the shift: capital X is x minus h, capital Y is y minus k.
Here is the compact toolkit for slope and angles — six facts that cover almost every question.
Slope equals tan of the inclination, valid for every line except the vertical one at ninety degrees.
From two points, slope is y two minus y one over x two minus x one, provided the x-values differ.
Parallel lines share the same slope: m one equals m two.
Perpendicular lines satisfy m one times m two equals minus one — flip and negate.
The angle between two lines is the inverse tangent of the modulus of m two minus m one over one plus m one m two.
Three points are collinear when the slope of A B equals the slope of B C.
And a handy special case: a line equally inclined to both axes has slope plus or minus one, since its inclination is forty five or one hundred thirty five degrees.
Here is the complete family of line equations on one board — your reference for the whole subtopic.
A horizontal line is y equals b; a vertical line is x equals a. These are the two that slope cannot handle.
Point-slope: y minus y one equals m times x minus x one. This is the parent of the whole family.
Two-point form is the same, with the slope written as y two minus y one over x two minus x one.
Slope-intercept: y equals m x plus c, ready to read off slope and y-intercept at a glance.
Intercept form: x over a plus y over b equals one, using the two axis crossings directly.
Normal form: x cos omega plus y sin omega equals p, with p the non-negative distance from the origin.
And the universal fallback, general form: A x plus B y plus C equals zero.
From that general form, read off the slope as minus A over B, the x-intercept as minus C over A, and the y-intercept as minus C over B.
Here is the compact toolkit for every distance question in this chapter.
Point to line: d is the modulus of A x one plus B y one plus C, over the root of A squared plus B squared. The line must be in general form first.
Parallel lines: d is the modulus of C one minus C two over the same root.
But only after normalizing both lines to identical A and B — this is the single most common slip, so write it on your hand.
The symmetric form: x minus x one over cos theta equals y minus y one over sin theta equals r.
Here r is the signed distance from the base point along the inclination theta — the parameter is the ruler.
And the side test: just look at the sign of A x one plus B y one plus C.
Same sign for two points means they are on the same side; opposite signs mean the line runs between them.
Let's close distances with the four traps that quietly drain marks.
Trap one, the big one: skipping normalization for parallel lines. The constant-difference formula is valid only when both lines show identical A and B, so rescale one first, every time.
Trap two: distance is never negative, so keep the modulus in the point-to-line formula. The signed version is useful, but it is not the distance.

Trap three: the denominator is the root of A squared plus B squared — not A squared plus B squared, and not the sum of the absolute values. It is the same root-sum-of-squares you met in the normal form.
Trap four: in the symmetric form, only the genuine unit direction, cos theta and sin theta, makes the parameter r equal the true distance.
<whisper>And the pro-tip worth its weight in marks: the sign of the signed distance tells you which side of the line a point sits on.</whisper>
Two points with the same sign lie on the same side; opposite signs mean the line runs between them.
That one idea settles questions like 'are these on the same side?' and even 'is the origin inside this triangle?' with no extra construction at all.
Here is the toolkit for intersection, parallelism, concurrency, and the family trick.
The intersection point by Cramer's rule: x is b one c two minus b two c one, over a one b two minus a two b one; y has the same denominator with c one a two minus c two a one on top.
Two lines are parallel and distinct when the a-ratio equals the b-ratio but differs from the c-ratio.
They intersect when the a-ratio is not equal to the b-ratio.
And they are coincident when all three ratios are equal — the same line written twice.
Three lines are concurrent when the three by three determinant of their coefficients is zero.
And the family through a junction is L one plus lambda L two equals zero.
One standing caveat: the concurrency test assumes no two of the three lines are parallel, so always sanity-check that.
Here is the whole toolkit for angle bisectors on one board.
The pair of bisectors: the first line over its root equals plus or minus the second line over its root.
Before anything else, normalize: make both constant terms positive.
With that done, the plus sign is the bisector of the angle containing the origin.
For acute versus obtuse, look at a one a two plus b one b two: positive means the plus bisector is obtuse, negative means the plus bisector is acute.
But only bother with this when the question actually asks acute or obtuse — do not compute it out of habit.
And always, the slopes of the two bisectors multiply to minus one.
Finally, remember each line keeps its own root of a squared plus b squared in the denominator; do not share one across both.
Here is the whole toolkit for feet, images and reflections.
The foot: x minus x one over a equals y minus y one over b equals minus a x one plus b y one plus c, over a squared plus b squared.
The image is the same, with a factor of two on that numerator — twice the step.
And the anchor relating them: the foot is the midpoint of the point and its image.
For the special mirror y equals x, just swap the coordinates.
For the x-axis, negate the y-coordinate.
For the y-axis, negate the x-coordinate.
